newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh half-year growth about five percent.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh half-year growth about five percent.

text.p: Bangladesh's economic growth in first half of fiscal 1996/97 has been about five percent year-on-year, Finance Ministry officials said on Friday.
They said the highest growth achieved during the July-December period was more than nine percent in agriculture, and the lowest was three percent in the energy sector.
Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria, presenting the national budget last July, predicted overall 1996/97 economic growth of between six and seven percent.
But achieving that might be difficult because of three major obstacles, a senior Finance Ministry official said.

Firstly, Bangladesh, which normally exports fertiliser, was forced to make huge imports after the state-run Chittagong Urea Fertiliser Ltd plant halted production due to a shortage of natural gas used as raw material. Problems in other fertiliser plants exacerbated the shortage.
"Total (urea) imports this year may be around 200,000 tonnes," one official said without giving details.
Secondly, while petroleum prices in the international market increased by about 20 percent, Bangladesh had to keep domestic prices unchanged to avoid "political consequences", he said.

Thirdly, the country's economy had to absorb shocks due to turbulence in the capital market. The all-share price index at the Dhaka Stock Exchange dropped to 1,879.58 on Thursday from over 3,600 two months ago.
"All these have affected the economy badly. Even at the end of the financial year the economy may not achieve the targeted growth rate (six percent)," the official told Reuters.
Kibria told parliament on Wednesday that foreign exchange reserves at the Bangladesh Bank, the central bank, were $1.86 billion on December 31, compared to $2.36 billion at the end of 1995.

Bangladesh Bank governor Lutfar Rahman Sarker told Reuters that during the first five months (July-November) of the current fiscal year, debt payments were $138 million, up from $110.40 million in the corresponding period of 1995/96.
There were other reasons for a reduction in the reserves, a Finance Ministry official said.
He said the number of foreign visits by government ministers and officials had increased since Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina came to power last June, adding to pressure on the reserves.
Kibria told parliament on Wednesday that during July-November, export earnings totalled $1.65 billion compared to $1.53 billion in the corresponding period of 1995/96.
Remittances from expatriate workers totalled $695 million during the five months, compared to $580 million in the same period in the previous year.
